passage:
Warden's note, Boys' Hostel B, 20 July
Rahil, second year, came to me asking if he could skip the mess and cook instant noodles in his room to "save money". He has also been walking forty minutes to college instead of taking the bus, for the same reason.
Last week, though, his internship bonus came through, and within days he had bought new headphones and a gaming chair, and treated the whole floor to dinner. When I asked, he said, "That was bonus money, ma'am. The bus fare comes from my real money."
He honestly doesn't see it as one pot. I didn't lecture. I asked him to write every rupee he has, from anywhere, on one sheet. His classmate Deepika, who keeps a simple notebook budget, offered to sit with him. They will meet on Sunday. I'll check in next week.
Farida

qa.q: What did Rahil buy after the internship bonus came through?
qa.a: He bought new headphones and a gaming chair, and treated the whole floor to dinner.

qa.q: Why does walking forty minutes feel sensible to Rahil while the gaming chair doesn't feel wasteful?
qa.a: Rahil feels relaxed about spending the bonus because in his mind it is a separate extra pot, while he feels protective of his "real money" and guards the bus fare tightly.

qa.q: What does Farida's one-sheet idea help Rahil see?
qa.a: Writing every rupee on one sheet shows all his money as one pot, so he can see the bonus could have covered a lot of bus rides and mess meals.

qa.q: How might Deepika see Rahil's habits when they sit together?
qa.a: Deepika may find it surprising that someone skipping the bus to save money just spent so much on a chair, and will probably help Rahil see it as one budget.

grounding: It shows a male student spending a bonus freely while pinching on bus fare and meals, because separate mental pots hide his whole picture.

passage:
Wednesday, 9 pm
Had dry bread and tea for dinner again to save forty rupees on the mess extra. I've been proud of this streak. I also skipped photocopying the notes and took photos instead, to save ten.
Then I opened my bank app to check something and saw it: the tax refund from my summer job came in three weeks ago, and I've spent almost all of it. New sneakers. A concert ticket. Snacks for everyone at Tanuja's birthday. I barely remember deciding any of it. It just felt like bonus money, not "mine".
Nikita didi called and I told her. She laughed and said, "Little brother, you're guarding coins and throwing notes." She's right. It's all one wallet.
Tomorrow: one list of everything, refund included.
Aniket

qa.q: What came into Aniket's account three weeks ago?
qa.a: The tax refund from the summer job came in three weeks ago.

qa.q: Why did the refund not feel like Aniket's own money?
qa.a: The refund felt like bonus money, so Aniket spent it carelessly without guilt, while saving forty rupees on dinner made him feel proud of his careful effort.

qa.q: Is Aniket's plan for tomorrow a good start?
qa.a: Yes; putting everything, refund included, on one list lets Aniket see the whole picture and notice the snacks and sneakers cost far more than the savings on meals.

qa.q: What does Nikita didi's line about coins and notes show about how she sees it?
qa.a: She sees the mismatch clearly and finds it a bit funny, but cares enough to point out that all the money comes from one wallet.

grounding: It shows a young man spending a tax refund carelessly while pinching on small daily costs, because he keeps the money in separate mental accounts.

1 March. Arnab and his wife Kalyani sat at the dining table in their Kolkata flat with one sheet of paper. Savings, the scooter loan, what the credit card owed, the small fund her father had left her: everything went on it, and at the bottom, one number. "That's us," Arnab said.
14 March. Arnab's work bonus arrived. Kalyani grinned. "Free money! Beach trip?" Arnab laughed. "It's not free, it's just more of the same pool. But the trip is on our list anyway." They moved part of it into the savings account they had labelled "Trip", and the rest into "Emergency".
31 March. They checked what had come in and gone out that month. Food deliveries had doubled. Nobody panicked. They just planned more home dinners for April.

qa.q: What did Arnab and Kalyani write at the bottom of the sheet?
qa.a: At the bottom they wrote one number, for everything together.

qa.q: How does Arnab feel about the bonus when he says "it's just more of the same pool"?
qa.a: Arnab feels calm and steady about it; he sees every rupee as part of one whole, so he is happy to plan the trip but chooses it on purpose rather than treating the bonus as play money.

qa.q: How do the labelled accounts help rather than trap them?
qa.a: They are used as tools for goals, like Trip and Emergency, after looking at the whole picture, so the labels guide saving without hiding the full number.

qa.q: How might Kalyani feel about the end-of-March check?
qa.a: She likely feels calm rather than scolded, since nobody panicked and the fix was simply more home dinners.

grounding: It shows an earner treating all money as one pool, tracking the total and monthly flow, and using labelled accounts only as tools for goals.

passage:
Karthik, you've just got your first proper salary, so let me tell you what I learned the hard way. At your age I had five little tins in my head. Salary was for rent. My Diwali bonus was for gadgets. The money my father sent was for "emergencies", which somehow meant trips. I felt rich in one tin and broke in another, all in the same week.
Then an old accountant in our office, Mr. D'Cruz, asked me one day, "Asif, how much are you worth, in total?" I had no idea. That stung.
From that month I wrote everything on one page: what I owned, what I owed, what came in, what went out. Once a month, same Sunday. I still kept labelled envelopes, one for my sister's wedding, one for rainy days, but I knew they were all parts of one pile.
It's not about being stingy, beta. It's about seeing.

qa.q: What question did Mr. D'Cruz ask Asif?
qa.a: He asked, "Asif, how much are you worth, in total?"

qa.q: How did Asif feel on realising there was no answer to that question?
qa.a: Asif felt stung and exposed, seeing that the separate tins had hidden the full picture.

qa.q: What habit is Asif passing on to Karthik?
qa.a: Writing what is owned, owed, coming in and going out on one page once a month, and using labelled envelopes only as parts of one pile for clear goals.

qa.q: Why might Karthik find this story useful right now?
qa.a: Karthik has just got a first proper salary, so starting with one clear picture could save years of feeling rich and broke in the same week.

grounding: It shows an elder, Asif, recalling learning to see all money as one pool, track the total and monthly flow, and use labelled envelopes only for goals.

The landlord's message came on Monday: rent going up from next month. On Tuesday, Nilesh reminded Gurleen that their cousin's wedding was in three weeks and gifts were expected. And her laptop had started dying.
The old Gurleen would have panicked in three separate directions. Instead she opened the spreadsheet she updated on the first of every month: everything she had, everything she owed, what came in, what went out. One sheet, one picture.
"Okay," she told Nilesh over the phone, the pressure cooker whistling behind her. "The wedding pot has less than we planned and the laptop pot is empty, but overall we're not in trouble. I'll move some from the travel pot to the laptop. The gift stays modest."
"You're not stressed?"
"I am. But I can see all of it. That's different."

qa.q: When did the landlord's message come?
qa.a: The landlord's message came on Monday.

qa.q: What does Gurleen mean by "I can see all of it. That's different"?
qa.a: She still feels stress, but seeing her whole picture on one sheet makes the problems feel manageable instead of scattered and frightening.

qa.q: How did Gurleen use her labelled pots wisely under pressure?
qa.a: She checked the whole picture first, then moved money between pots, from travel to laptop, treating the labels as tools rather than walls.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel hearing Gurleen's plan?
qa.a: Nilesh would likely feel reassured, since a stressful week of rent, a wedding and a dying laptop turned into a clear, calm plan.

grounding: It shows an earner who keeps one full monthly picture of money and uses labelled pots flexibly as tools when several costs arrive at once.

passage:
"Siddiq, listen," Mum called from the kitchen of their Cape Town flat. "Swimming towel, give Thabo back his book, tell Ms Adams you'll be late on Friday, bring the permission slip, and don't forget your lunch tin this time."
"Okay!" Siddiq shouted, already pulling on his shoes.
At school he had his towel. That was it. Thabo asked about the book, and Siddiq stared at him. "Mum said something about a book..." The lunch tin stayed in the classroom again.
That evening Mum sighed, then tore off a sticky note. "Three things for tomorrow," she said, writing them one under the other. "Book. Slip. Tin. Stick it on your bag."
The next day Siddiq ticked off all three and brought the note home proudly.

qa.q: What was the only thing Siddiq had at school?
qa.a: Siddiq had his towel. That was it.

qa.q: Why didn't Siddiq remember the rest even though he said "Okay!"?
qa.a: He wasn't being careless on purpose; five instructions called out at once were more than he could hold in mind while rushing, so only the first one stuck.

qa.q: What made Mum's second try work?
qa.a: She gave just three short items, wrote them one under the other, and put the note on his bag, so he didn't have to hold them all in memory.

qa.q: How does Thabo experience the forgotten book?
qa.a: Thabo is left waiting for the book, and is probably puzzled when Siddiq only half remembers Mum saying something about it.

grounding: It shows a child forgetting most of a long list of instructions and managing fine once given a few short written steps.

passage:
In the science lab, the teacher read the steps at top speed: "Pour fifty millilitres of water into the beaker, add two spoons of salt, stir till it dissolves, dip the thread, tie it to the pencil, rest the pencil across the top, label it with your name, and put it on the window sill."
Yash nodded along. When the class began, he poured the water, added the salt, then stood with the thread in his hand, stuck. What came after stirring? Aadhya, at the next table, was just as lost.
"Let's do it one at a time," she whispered, and went to read the board, where the teacher had now written the steps as a numbered list. "Step three: stir." "Done." "Step four: dip the thread."
Ten minutes later both beakers stood labelled on the window sill.

qa.q: Where did the beakers go at the end?
qa.a: Both beakers stood labelled on the window sill.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling as he stood with the thread in his hand?
qa.a: He felt stuck and confused, because the long list read at top speed hadn't stayed in his head past the first few steps.

qa.q: How could the teacher give instructions so more students can follow them?
qa.a: Give a few short steps at a time, or write them as a numbered list from the start, so students can check each step instead of holding all eight in memory.

qa.q: What is it like for Aadhya to realise she is just as lost?
qa.a: It may be a relief to know Yash is stuck too, and it pushes her to find a way through by reading the steps one by one.

grounding: It shows children who lose track of a long list of spoken lab steps and succeed once they follow short numbered steps one at a time.

passage:
I'm Sachin. Yesterday Amma gave my sister Chandrika a job while rushing to the office: "Take the clothes off the line, fold the towels, put Appa's shirts on the bed, water the tulsi, and switch the geyser on at six." Chandrika said yes to everything.
When I came home she had taken in the clothes and was sitting on the pile, looking confused. The shirts were still mixed with the towels. The tulsi was dry. I don't know exactly what was in her head, but she looked like she was trying to remember and couldn't.
I asked, "What did Amma say?" She said, "Clothes... and something about six?"
So I made it simple. "First, fold the towels. Then tell me." One thing at a time, she finished everything before Amma got back.

qa.q: What was Chandrika doing when Sachin came home?
qa.a: She was sitting on the pile of clothes, looking confused.

qa.q: How was Chandrika feeling when she answered "Clothes... and something about six?"
qa.a: Chandrika was confused and overwhelmed; she really tried to remember but could hold only a couple of the five jobs, not because she didn't care.

qa.q: Which approach worked, and why?
qa.a: Sachin's one-thing-at-a-time steps worked, because Chandrika only had to hold one small job in mind before checking back.

qa.q: What would change if Amma had written the jobs down before leaving?
qa.a: Chandrika could have looked at the list instead of relying on memory, and the tulsi and shirts might have been done before Sachin got home.

grounding: It shows a child who forgets most of a long list of chores and finishes them all once they are given as short, single steps.

In the corner of his room in a Lajpat Nagar flat, Ojas had his chemistry book open at the mole concept, earphones in, a Punjabi playlist singing loudly in his ears. His phone lay beside the book, buzzing every few seconds with the class group arguing about a cricket match.
He read the definition of a mole. Buzz. He replied with a laughing face. Read it again. A chorus in his ear made him hum along. By ten o'clock he had read the same page six times and could not have explained a single line.
Next morning, in the unit test, the question on moles looked completely new. Trisha, beside him, was writing steadily. She had revised in the silent reading room downstairs, phone in her bag.

qa.q: How many times had Ojas read the same page by ten o'clock?
qa.a: He had read the same page six times.

qa.q: Why did the mole question look completely new to Ojas?
qa.a: His attention kept being pulled away by the buzzing phone and the lyrics, so nothing from the page settled into memory, even though he felt he had studied.

qa.q: What could Ojas change the next time he revises?
qa.a: Put the phone in another room, switch to silence or music without words, and study in short focused blocks, maybe in the reading room like Trisha.

qa.q: How might Trisha see the difference between their evenings?
qa.a: Trisha probably realises her quiet hour with the phone put away gave her more than Ojas got from a long, noisy evening.

grounding: It shows a teenager studying with a buzzing phone and lyrics in his ears whose chemistry doesn't stick because his attention is overloaded.

I'm Santosh. In Class 11 I had a habit I was proud of: I could study, chat and listen to rap all at the same time. I'd tell Hansa, "Multitasking, yaar." Hansa just shook her head.
Then came the physics half-yearly. I had spent whole evenings "revising" circular motion, but in the exam the formulas were mush. I knew I had seen them. I just couldn't find them.
Hansa had studied fewer hours than me and scored way higher. She told me she put her phone in a drawer and kept things quiet for fifty minutes at a stretch.
I tried it the next month, grumbling. No lyrics, no pings. It was boring at first. But in the next test the formulas were just there, as if they had been waiting for me.

qa.q: Which topic had Santosh been revising before the half-yearly?
qa.a: Santosh had been revising circular motion.

qa.q: Why was Santosh proud of studying, chatting and listening to rap together?
qa.a: It felt efficient and clever, like getting more done, so Santosh didn't notice the overload was stopping the formulas from sticking.

qa.q: What worked for Hansa, and could it work for others?
qa.a: Putting the phone in a drawer and keeping things quiet for fifty minutes at a stretch; it gives attention one job, which helps memory for most people.

qa.q: What might Hansa have thought when Santosh said "Multitasking"?
qa.a: Hansa probably thought it wasn't working but didn't want to argue, which is why the only answer was a shake of the head.

grounding: It shows a teenager whose physics revision didn't stick while studying with chat and lyrics, because attention and memory were overloaded.

In Barshi, Kiran spent mornings at college, afternoons behind the counter of the family's seed shop, and nights with a torch over accounts textbooks. Exams started Monday. Amma's knee was getting worse and the monsoon was late, so sales were down. Kiran thought about all of it at once, all the time.
On Thursday Salma, a regular customer, paid for two bags of seed. Kiran gave her change for a hundred instead of fifty. She came back smiling and returned the extra. "You're somewhere else today."
That night Kiran filled in the practice form and wrote the wrong roll number twice. Kiran's head felt full of cotton.
Salma's words stuck. The next morning Kiran wrote a list: shop hours cut to three days till exams, a cousin to cover, one worry at a time.

qa.q: What mistake did Kiran make with Salma's change?
qa.a: Kiran gave her change for a hundred instead of fifty.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling on the night of the wrong roll number?
qa.a: Kiran felt foggy and overloaded, head full of cotton, because exams, the shop and worries about Amma and the rain were all taking up space at once.

qa.q: Is Kiran's list a good response?
qa.a: Yes; cutting shop hours, asking a cousin to cover and taking one worry at a time frees some mental space, which should cut down the careless mistakes.

qa.q: How did Salma see Kiran that day?
qa.a: Salma noticed Kiran was distracted and "somewhere else", and responded kindly by returning the money with a smile.

grounding: It shows a student juggling exams, shop work and family worries who makes careless mistakes and feels foggy because stress uses up mental capacity.

In Porto, Ivan had three exams in five days, four evening shifts at the café near the university, and a letter about his residence permit renewal that he kept rereading at night. By Wednesday he was running on coffee and dread.
At the café he rang up a cappuccino as a latte, then forgot a table entirely. Beatriz, his shift partner, quietly fixed both. At home he emailed his statistics assignment to his economics professor.
"You look like a phone with too many apps open," Beatriz said at closing.
"I'm fine. I just need to push through."
"You're not dumb, you're full." She took his notepad and wrote three things: swap Friday shift, call the international office about the permit, exam first.
Ivan read the list twice. It was the first thing all week that let him breathe out.

qa.q: Where did Ivan send his statistics assignment?
qa.a: He emailed his statistics assignment to his economics professor.

qa.q: Why does Ivan insist he just needs to push through?
qa.a: He probably feels he should cope alone and doesn't see the mistakes as a sign of overload; admitting it might feel like weakness.

qa.q: Why does Beatriz's three-item list help?
qa.a: It takes the permit worry and an extra shift off his mind, so his limited attention can go to the exam first.

qa.q: How does Beatriz see Ivan's mistakes?
qa.a: Beatriz sees them as a sign he is overloaded, not careless or dumb, like a phone with too many apps open.

By the second week of placements, the hostel corridor smelled of instant coffee and panic. Chinmay had two interviews, a final-year project review, and a phone that buzzed with updates about his grandfather in hospital back in Nagpur.

passage:
Dear Uday,
You said your first month at work feels like drowning, little brother. Mine did too. Here's what finally helped your akka, in case it helps you.
One: I write everything down. The moment someone asks me something, it goes in a notebook, not in my head.
Two: big jobs get chopped. "Finish the audit report" became six tiny steps, and I only look at the next one.
Three: I turned off every notification except calls from Amma and my manager. Group chats get checked at lunch and at five.
Four: every ninety minutes I walk to the water cooler and back. Sounds silly. It isn't.
Last week I finished the audit two days early and still had room in my head for the tricky part, the one that mattered.
Try one thing, not all four.
Love,
Harsha

qa.q: Which calls does Harsha still let through?
qa.a: Harsha still lets through calls from Amma and the manager.

qa.q: Why do you think Harsha tells Uday to try one thing, not all four?
qa.a: Harsha remembers how overwhelming the first month felt and doesn't want the advice itself to become one more heavy load.

qa.q: Which of Harsha's habits might help Uday most in a drowning week, and why?
qa.a: Writing everything down is a strong first step, because it frees his head from holding every request and leaves room for the important work.

qa.q: How might Uday feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: Uday would likely feel less alone 🙂, knowing his akka struggled too and found simple ways through it.

grounding: It shows a young woman who writes things down, breaks big jobs into steps, cuts notifications and takes breaks so she can focus on what matters.

passage:
Bidisha, thanks for having me. People ask how I, Nazia, a girl from Malda, handle a hospital admin job with a hundred things flying at me. Honestly, I used to be a mess. Sticky notes everywhere, eighty tabs open, phone buzzing through every meeting. I once forgot to book an ambulance transfer because a group chat about cake distracted me.
That scared me. So I changed four things. Everything goes into one list the second it comes in. Big jobs, like the new staff rota, get broken into steps so small they're almost silly. All app notifications are off, except the hospital pager. And I take a real break outside twice a day, even when I think I can't.
The funny thing? I'm faster now. The important stuff, the patient transfers, gets my full brain instead of the leftovers.

qa.q: What distracted Nazia on the day the transfer was forgotten?
qa.a: A group chat about cake distracted her.

qa.q: Why did forgetting the ambulance transfer scare Nazia so much?
qa.a: Nazia felt alarmed and shaken, because the forgotten transfer showed her that the clutter of notes, tabs and chats was crowding out something that could affect a patient.

qa.q: Which of Nazia's changes protects the important work best?
qa.a: Turning off all notifications except the pager, because it stops small interruptions from stealing attention from patient transfers.

qa.q: How might patients and families feel the difference in Nazia's work?
qa.a: Their transfers now get her full attention, so things are less likely to slip, which means fewer delays and more trust.

grounding: It shows a young woman who writes tasks down, breaks big jobs into steps, silences notifications and takes breaks to keep her mind on what matters.

I'm Chaitanya, and I sit across from Rukmini at our design firm in Kochi. Last quarter she was drowning like the rest of us: the brochure our manager Lalit kept chasing, three client calls a day, a chat window that never stopped blinking.
Then she changed things, and I watched. She started every morning by writing a short list in a notebook. She broke the brochure into small steps on sticky notes and moved them across her desk as she finished each one. Her chat went on "do not disturb" in two-hour blocks. At eleven and at four she got up and walked around the building.
I can't say what was going on in her head, but she stopped looking frazzled. She finished the brochure a day early, and it was the cleanest work on the team.

qa.q: Where did Rukmini move her sticky notes?
qa.a: She moved them across her desk as she finished each one.

qa.q: What might Rukmini have been feeling before she changed things?
qa.a: She was probably overwhelmed and scattered, drowning in calls, chat messages and a big brochure all at once.

qa.q: Which of Rukmini's habits could the rest of the team copy most easily?
qa.a: The two-hour "do not disturb" blocks and the short walks at eleven and four, which protect focus and give the mind a rest.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see the change in Rukmini?
qa.a: Chaitanya notices she stopped looking frazzled and did the cleanest work on the team, and seems impressed, though unsure what she felt inside.

grounding: It shows, through a colleague's eyes, a young woman lightening her mental load with lists, small steps, fewer notifications and breaks.

passage:
Supervisor's note, customer support floor, week 1
Nandini joined on Monday. By Tuesday afternoon she was sitting with four manuals open, three screens of the ticket system, and a face that said she had stopped understanding anything around noon. When a customer asked a simple refund question, she froze and put him on hold for five minutes.
My fault, partly. I gave her the whole system in one day.
So I started again. Today we did only refunds. I showed her two real past tickets, one easy and one tricky, and gave her a one-page checklist. She handled six refund calls with me listening in, and by the last one she didn't look at the checklist once.
Plan: one new ticket type every two days, with examples and practice, before we add anything more.
Farida

qa.q: How long did Nandini put the customer on hold?
qa.a: She put him on hold for five minutes.

qa.q: What does Nandini's face on Tuesday afternoon suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt overwhelmed and lost, with too much new information to hold, so even a simple question became hard.

qa.q: What did Farida change, and why did it work?
qa.a: Farida taught one ticket type at a time with real examples, a one-page checklist and practice calls, so Nandini could master refunds before anything new was added.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel after handling six refund calls?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and more confident 😊, since by the last call she no longer needed the checklist.

grounding: It shows a senior colleague who sees a new hire overloaded and switches to teaching in small stages with examples, a checklist and practice.

Thursday, late
New intern Alka started at the lab this week and I nearly broke her. On day one I walked her through the whole sample-tracking system, the safety sheets, the ordering process and the freezer map. Forty minutes, non-stop. She nodded and took notes. Today she labelled a whole rack with last year's codes and then apologised about eight times.
Not her fault. I remember my own first week; I cried in the washroom.
So this afternoon I slowed right down. Just labelling. I did two racks with her watching, gave her a checklist with a photo of a correct label, and let her do the third alone while I stayed nearby. Perfect.
Tomorrow: the freezer map, nothing else.
Bhupen

qa.q: What did Alka label with last year's codes?
qa.a: Alka labelled a whole rack with last year's codes.

qa.q: Why did Alka apologise about eight times?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and worried about making a bad impression, not realising the mistake came from being given too much at once.

qa.q: What did Bhupen's afternoon approach include?
qa.a: Just one task, a demonstration on two racks, a checklist with a photo of a correct label, and a chance to practise alone with Bhupen nearby.

qa.q: Why might Bhupen understand Alka so well?
qa.a: Bhupen remembers crying in the washroom in a first week, so Alka's overwhelm feels familiar rather than annoying.

grounding: It shows a senior colleague noticing a new intern drowning in information and switching to small stages with a demonstration, checklist and practice.

passage:
In their Copenhagen flat, Anders, two, was stacking wooden blocks into a wobbly tower, tongue between his teeth. "Anders! Bath time!" his father, Emil, called from the hallway. Nothing. "Anders!" Louder. The tower grew one block taller.
Emil felt a flash of irritation, then came and knelt beside him and touched his shoulder. Anders looked up, surprised, as if he had only now noticed his papa. "Tower!" he said proudly.
"Big tower," Emil agreed. "One more block, then bath."

qa.q: What was Anders building?
qa.a: Anders was stacking wooden blocks into a wobbly tower.

qa.q: Why didn't Anders answer when Emil called?
qa.a: He was so absorbed in the tower that the call didn't reach him; his surprised look shows he truly hadn't noticed, not that he was ignoring his papa.

qa.q: What worked for Emil?
qa.a: Going close, touching Anders gently, sharing interest in the tower, and giving one small step before bath.

qa.q: How might the evening go if Emil kept calling from the hallway?
qa.a: Emil would likely get more irritated, and Anders might be startled or upset when finally pulled away, turning bath time into a fight.

grounding: It shows a toddler so absorbed in his blocks that he does not hear his name, a normal attention limit rather than defiance.

passage: I'm Himani, Pallavi's neighbour. Yesterday on the building lawn, her son Neel, who is two, was pouring sand from one cup into another, again and again. Then she walked over and tapped him, and he jumped a little and smiled at her as if she had just appeared. I don't think he had heard her at all.

qa.q: What could Pallavi do first the next time she needs Neel's attention?
qa.a: Walk over, get down to his level and touch him gently before speaking, since calling from far away may not reach him.

qa.q: How did Himani's view of Neel change?
qa.a: Himani first thought he was being stubborn, then saw his surprised smile and realised he hadn't heard at all.

grounding: It shows a toddler so absorbed in pouring sand that he does not hear his name, which a neighbour first mistakes for stubbornness.

The temple fair was loud: drums, bells, a balloon seller shouting. Santosh, five, sat on the mat in front of the puppet stage while his mother, Hansa, searched the nearby steps for his lost sandal, glancing back at him every few seconds.
She found it and walked past the stage waving it, calling his name. His eyes stayed on the king puppet's golden crown. She passed again with a water bottle, right in front of him. Nothing.
When the show ended he turned and saw her. "Amma, you went away!"
"Kanna, I walked past you twice!"
He shook his head, very sure. "No. Only the king was there."

qa.a: His eyes stayed on the king puppet's golden crown.

qa.q: Why was Santosh so sure his mother had gone away?

qa.q: What could Hansa do at the next busy show?
qa.a: Sit beside him or touch his shoulder when she comes back, instead of expecting him to notice her walking by in the noise.

qa.q: What is it like for Hansa when Santosh says she went away?
qa.a: She is probably surprised and a little amused 😅, since she walked right past him twice while keeping an eye on him.

grounding: It shows a preschooler at a noisy fair who misses his mother walking past twice because his attention is fixed on the puppet show.

In the colony hall in Chennai, the Sunday puppet show had begun. Sonali, five, sat in the front row as the crow puppet tried to steal the grandmother's vadai.
Behind the rows, her father, Saurabh, walked slowly across the hall carrying a huge red balloon he had bought for her. He even stopped and bounced it near the front. Other children pointed. Sonali didn't turn.
After the show he held out the balloon. "Did you see me walk past?"
Sonali's eyes went wide. "When? You weren't here!"
"I was right there, with this big red thing."
She stared at the balloon as if it had appeared by magic.

qa.q: What was Saurabh carrying across the hall?
qa.a: He was carrying a huge red balloon he had bought for Sonali.

qa.q: Why did Sonali stare at the balloon as if it had appeared by magic?
qa.a: Sonali was surprised and amazed, because her attention had been so fixed on the crow and the vadai that she never saw the balloon until it appeared in front of her.

qa.q: What could Saurabh learn about getting Sonali's attention?
qa.a: When she is deep in something, even a big red balloon may not register; going close and speaking to her directly works better.

qa.q: Why might the other children have noticed Saurabh when Sonali didn't?
qa.a: They weren't as locked onto the puppets at that moment, so the balloon caught their eye, while Sonali's attention had no room left for it.

grounding: It shows a preschooler absorbed in a puppet show who misses her father walking past with a balloon, as attention pulls to one focus.

passage:
Salma, you think you notice everything? Let me tell you what happened to your Kiran Mama at ten. Our science sir wheeled a TV and a video player into class, a big event in our Bhopal school. On the screen, students in white and black shirts were passing a ball. "Count the passes by the white team," he said. I counted like my life depended on it. Fifteen! I was so proud.
Then sir asked, "Who saw the tiger?" Half the class laughed. I thought they were joking. He rewound it, and there it was: a person in a tiger costume strolling right through the middle, even waving. I had looked straight at that screen and never seen it.
Sir said, "You were looking, but your mind was busy counting." I've never forgotten that.

qa.q: How many passes did Kiran Mama count?
qa.a: Kiran Mama counted fifteen passes.

qa.q: Why did young Kiran think the class was joking about the tiger?
qa.a: Kiran was so absorbed in counting the passes, and so proud of getting fifteen, that the tiger never registered, and he felt certain there had been nothing to see.

qa.q: What lesson could Salma take from this story?
qa.a: Salma could remember that focusing hard on one thing can hide other things, so it helps to look again or check with others before being sure.

qa.q: What was it like for the classmates who spotted the tiger?
qa.a: They found it funny and were surprised others missed it, probably not realising they could miss things just as easily when focused.

grounding: It shows, through an uncle's memory, a child counting passes in a video who never sees a costumed tiger cross the screen.

The power had gone out in their Gangtok lane, and Pema's laptop was down to eight percent. "Quick, before it dies," Pema said. "The science club video. Count the passes by the red team."
Ira leaned in, a finger tapping each pass. Rain drummed on the tin roof. Pema held the torch, not counting, just watching.
"Eleven!" Ira shouted as the clip ended.
"Correct. And the panda?"
"What panda?"
Pema pressed replay with two percent left. A person in a panda suit walked slowly through the players, stopped in the middle, and beat its chest. Ira's mouth fell open. "That wasn't there!"
The screen went black. "It was," Pema said, laughing in the dark. "You just weren't looking for it."

qa.q: How many passes did Ira count?
qa.a: Ira counted eleven passes by the red team.

qa.q: Why was Ira so sure the panda "wasn't there"?
qa.a: Ira's attention was fully on counting the red team's passes, so the panda never reached awareness, and missing it felt like proof it wasn't there 🤔.

qa.q: What could Ira try the next time a video asks for careful counting?
qa.a: Watch once for the task and once more just looking at everything, since attention on one job can hide surprises.

qa.q: Why did Pema see the panda when Ira didn't?
qa.a: Pema was holding the torch and not counting, so Pema's attention was free to notice the panda walking through.

grounding: It shows a child counting passes in a video who misses a person in a panda suit, because attention, not the eyes alone, decides what is seen.

In Mrs. Pillai's Class 6 in Thane, the smart board showed two teams tossing a basketball. "Count the passes by the blue shirts," she said. "No talking."
Saurabh counted under his breath, fingers twitching with each pass. Chetan, beside him, was counting too, lips moving. The clip was only a minute long.
"Sixteen," Saurabh said. "Seventeen," said Chetan.
"Close," said Mrs. Pillai. "Now, who saw the gorilla?"
The room exploded. A few children waved their hands. Saurabh and Chetan looked at each other, baffled. She played it again, and a person in a gorilla suit strolled into the middle, thumped their chest, and walked off.
"No way," Saurabh whispered. "I was looking right there."
"That," said Mrs. Pillai, "is exactly the point."

qa.q: Whose passes were the children told to count?
qa.a: They were told to count the passes by the blue shirts.

qa.q: What does Saurabh's whisper "I was looking right there" show he felt?
qa.a: He felt amazed and a bit unsettled, realising that looking straight at something isn't the same as noticing it when attention is busy counting.

qa.q: How could Mrs. Pillai use this moment to help the class?
qa.a: She could explain that attention picks what we notice, and suggest pausing to look around when very focused, for example before crossing a road.

qa.q: What was it like for the children who did see the gorilla?
qa.a: They were excited and probably amused that others missed something so obvious, though they may have missed a pass or two themselves.

grounding: It shows children counting passes in a video who miss a person in a gorilla suit, showing that attention decides what is seen.
